question.value: Construct an extinction law from the near-infrared to the ultraviolet towards the cluster R136 in the LMC, measure extinction towards individual sources, map the spatial distribution of dust, and improve mass measurements of the very massive WNh stars.

evidence.quote: Our aims are to construct an extinction law towards R136, and to measure the extinction towards individual sources inside the cluster.
This will allow us to map the spatial distribution of the dust, to learn about dust properties, and to improve mass measurements of the very massive WNh stars inside the cluster.

method.value: Convert optical (HST/WFC3) and NIR (VLT/SPHERE) magnitudes to fluxes using SVO filter transmission curves, and bin flux-calibrated HST/STIS UV spectra into 9 synthetic passbands.

For the UV, we bin the observed flux points by taking the flux average over nine different wavelength regions as specified in 5.
With the 4 optical and 3 NIR photometry points for the R136 core stars, the observed SEDs consist of 16 flux points in total.

analysis_steps.goal: Compute intrinsic model SEDs for the R136 core stars

method.value: Compute non-LTE stellar atmosphere models using Fastwind adopting stellar parameters from Brands et al. (2022), scaling the output SED by stellar surface area to vary stellar radius.

evidence.quote: We compute models of intrinsic SEDs with the model atmosphere code Fastwind (cite: 1997A&A...323..488S; 2005A&A...435..669P; 2012A&A...537A..79R; 2016A&A...590A..88C; 2018A&A...619A..59S).
For the stellar parameters, we adopt the values of the optical and UV analysis of (cite: 2022arXiv220211080B) for stars in the core of R136.

assumptions.value: Small changes in stellar radius R_* do not significantly change the atmospheric structure, allowing R_* to be varied by scaling the model SED.

evidence.quote: However, for small changes in $R_*$, the structure of the atmosphere will not change significantly and this means that we can change $R_*$ of the model simply by multiplying the output SED with a factor that represents an increase or decrease in the stellar surface area.

validation.value: Tested mimicking the UV absorption-line forest with a 10% UV flux decrease (finding minor effect on c2 and none on A_5495, R_5495, L), and compared low mass-loss Fastwind models to hydrostatic TLUSTY models in U-B vs B-V and J-H vs H-K planes (differences <= 2% and <= 1%).

evidence.quote: We mimic the magnitude of the effect by representing the UV absorption-line forest by an overall decrease in the UV model flux of 10%. In this case, the best-fitting UV extinction is only slightly lower ($\Delta c_{2} = -0.05$)
We find that the qualitative behaviour of the two sets of models is similar, and that the absolute differences between the Fastwind and TLUSTY colours are never more than 2%.

Second, we compare the behaviour in the $J-H$ versus $H-K$ plane of the TLUSTY and Fastwind SEDs. Again, we find that the qualitative behaviour of the two sets of models is similar, and furthermore, that the differences are never larger than 1%.

analysis_steps.goal: Parameterise the modified NIR-to-UV extinction law and fit individual stellar SEDs

method.value: Construct a cubic spline extinction law in the optical/NIR based on Maíz Apellániz et al. (2014) and a UV parameterisation from Fitzpatrick & Massa (1990) with independent c2 and c4, then fit 5 free parameters per star to the observed SEDs.

evidence.quote: Briefly, we use the optical and NIR law of (cite: 2014AA...564A..63M), which we transform to the functional form of (cite: 1999PASP..111...63F). For the UV, we adopt the parameterisation of and (cite: 1990ApJS...72..163F).

We fit five parameters: $R_{5495}$, affecting the shape of the optical and NIR part of the curve; $c_2$ and $c_4$, relating to the UV part of the curve; the extinction in the $V$ band $A_V$; and the stellar angular radius $\theta_R = R_*/d$

We note that if we refit the SED while adopting a fixed value of $R_{5495}$(equal for all stars), we still recover the spatial trend for $A_{5495}$, although the gradient is slightly less steep.

findings_qualitative.value: There is a strong east-to-west spatial gradient in extinction (A_5495 and R_5495) across the 1 pc core of R136, coinciding with cold molecular gas (13CO) from an extension of the Stapler Nebula.

evidence.quote: We detect a strong spatial gradient in the extinction properties across the core of R136, coinciding with a gradient in density of cold gas that is part of an extension of the Stapler Nebula, a molecular cloud lying northeast of the cluster.

findings_qualitative.value: High values of R_V towards R136 are accompanied by relatively strong UV extinction with no significant trend between c_2 and R_5495, contrary to Galactic sightlines.

evidence.quote: However, the high values of $R_V$ are accompanied by relatively strong extinction in the ultraviolet, contrary to what is observed for Galactic sightlines.

evidence.loc: An R_5495-dependent average extinction law for R136
evidence.quote: The values show no significant trend as a function of $R_{5495}$, contrary to what is observed for Galactic sightlines (\[eq:fitz_uv_orig\]).

findings_qualitative.value: For R_V ~ 4.4, about three times (or a factor 2.5 at A_V = 1.0) fewer UV/ionising photons can escape relative to the canonical Galactic extinction law at the same R_V and A_V.

evidence.quote: For $R_{V} \sim 4.4$, about three times fewer ultraviolet photons can escape from the ambient dust environment relative to the canonical Galactic value of $R_{V} \sim 3.1$ at the same $A_{V}$.

At $A_V = 1.0$, the extinction towards R136 at UV wavelengths in the range $\lambda \approx 1700 - 1250$ Å is about one magnitude higher compared to the canonical Galactic extinction at the same $R_V$ and $A_V$, implying that the fraction of ionising photons that can escape is a factor 2.5 lower ($e^{\tau} \approx e^{A_V} \approx 0.4$).

claims.hypothesis: Does the extinction towards R136 follow the standard Galactic relation between optical slope (R_V) and UV extinction strength?
claims.experiment: Fit observed NIR-to-UV SEDs of 50 stars in the R136 core using Fastwind intrinsic models and a modified extinction law where optical slope R_5495 and UV slope c_2 are fitted independently.
claims.result: Obtained a high average R_V = 4.38 +/- 0.87 accompanied by strong UV extinction (average c_2 = 1.30 +/- 0.22) with no significant trend between c_2 and R_5495.
claims.finding: The Galactic relation between R_V and UV extinction does not hold in R136; dust properties towards R136 differ from the Milky Way, retaining a relatively large fraction of small grains despite high R_V.

evidence.quote: In line with previous measurements of R136 and the 30 Doradus region, we obtain a high total-to-relative extinction ($R_V = 4.38 \pm 0.87$). However, the high values of $R_V$ are accompanied by relatively strong extinction in the ultraviolet, contrary to what is observed for Galactic sightlines.

evidence.loc: An R_5495-dependent average extinction law for R136
evidence.quote: for which we find values in the range of $c_2 = 0.78-2.36$, with an average of $c_2 = 1.30\pm0.22$. The values show no significant trend as a function of $R_{5495}$, contrary to what is observed for Galactic sightlines (\[eq:fitz_uv_orig\]).

claims.hypothesis: Is the spatial gradient in extinction across the R136 core caused by foreground molecular cloud material from the Stapler Nebula?
claims.experiment: Map A_5495 and R_5495 spatially across the core and outskirts of R136 and compare with HST, JWST, and ALMA 13CO(2-1) column density maps.
claims.result: Extinction increases from A_5495 ~ 1.0 in the west to ~ 2.6 in the east, coinciding spatially with the eastern half of the cluster core where ALMA detects 13CO emission extending from the Stapler Nebula.
claims.finding: The extinction gradient across R136 is caused by dust grains within an extension of the Stapler Nebula molecular cloud stretching into the cluster core.

evidence.loc: Extinction due to an extension of the Stapler Nebula
evidence.quote: It is clear that in regions where $^{13}$CO is detected (eastern half of the cluster core), the extinction is higher, suggesting that this molecular cloud contains the dust grains that are causing the extinction gradient.

Comparing our extinction map to multi-wavelength observations of the same region, we conclude that the observed extinction gradient is likely caused by material belonging to an extension of a molecular cloud called the Stapler Nebula, which lies to the northeast of the cluster and stretches all the way to the R136 core.

claims.hypothesis: How do the revised extinction measurements affect the inferred luminosities and masses of the very massive WNh stars in R136?
claims.experiment: Re-derive luminosities from the SED fits and infer evolutionary and initial masses for R136a1, R136a2, and R136a3 using Bonnsai and single-star evolutionary tracks.
claims.result: Core star luminosities change by 0.03 dex on average; initial masses are 277 (+24/-27) M_odot for R136a1, 171 (+11/-7) M_odot for R136a2 (25% lower than Brands et al. 2022), and 209 (+10/-9) M_odot for R136a3.
claims.finding: Revised masses for R136a1 and R136a3 agree within uncertainties with previous values from Brands et al. (2022), while the mass of R136a2 is reduced by 25%.

evidence.quote: When accounting for the new values of the extinction, we find changes in luminosity of the R136 core stars of on average $0.03$ dex compared to the luminosities obtained by (cite: 2022arXiv220211080B)
We find that the evolutionary and initial masses we derive for R136a1 and R136a3 agree within uncertainties with those of (cite: 2022arXiv220211080B), while for R136a2 our masses are 25% lower.

why_this_data.value: 30 Doradus and R136 are proximate and relatively unobscured, allowing resolution of individual massive stars in a starburst-like environment to calibrate dust and stellar properties.

evidence.quote: The proximity of 30 Doradus and its relatively unobscured nature allow us to resolve the stellar population of this starburst-like environment.

why_this_method.value: Existing LMC and Galactic extinction laws fail to simultaneously fit the high optical R_V and strong UV extinction towards R136, and available data are too sparse to derive a completely new law from scratch, motivating a modification of existing laws using the 'extinction without standards' method.

evidence.quote: When considering the SED from the NIR to the UV, none of the existing extinction laws seem suitable for sightlines towards 30 Doradus.

The data we have available are insufficient to derive a completely new law: in the NIR and optical, we have only a few data points, and in the near-UV (between the $U$ band and the red end of the STIS/G140M grating at 1710 Å), we lack data altogether.
We therefore decided to modify an existing law.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Existing Galactic and LMC extinction laws (e.g. Fitzpatrick 1999, Cardelli et al. 1989, Fitzpatrick et al. 2019, Gordon et al. 2003, Howarth 1983, Pei 1992) were tested and rejected because they cannot simultaneously fit the optical/NIR and UV parts of the R136 SEDs.

evidence.quote: When considering the SED from the NIR to the UV, none of the existing extinction laws seem suitable for sightlines towards 30 Doradus.
Also, the Galactic laws, many of which allow for a varying $R_V$, are not suitable for 30 Doradus when the analysis is extended to the UV.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Deriving a completely new extinction law from scratch was rejected due to having too few photometric points in the NIR/optical and no data in the near-UV around the 2175 Å bump.

evidence.quote: The data we have available are insufficient to derive a completely new law: in the NIR and optical, we have only a few data points, and in the near-UV (between the $U$ band and the red end of the STIS/G140M grating at 1710 Å), we lack data altogether.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Leaving the UV parameter c_1 as a free parameter was tested and rejected because c_1 and c_2 are degenerate given the available data.

evidence.quote: This is because $c_2$ and $c_1$ are (to some extent) degenerate, and we do not have enough data to break this degeneracy. Experiments where we leave $c_1$ free in the fitting process show that, indeed, it is not possible to disentangle these two parameters with our data.

limitations_admitted.value: Pointing inaccuracies in the crowded HST/STIS long-slit observations leave flux calibration uncertainties of order 10% (up to a factor of two in extreme cases), and potential relative calibration divergence at lambda < 1400 Å may cause c_4 to be overestimated.

evidence.quote: As a consequence of pointing inaccuracies, uncertainties in the calibration remain; we estimate these to be on the order of 10% (see below), but in the most extreme cases they could be as large as a factor two.

If the low fluxes are due to an unknown calibration issue of the STIS spectra, and in reality the shape of the spectra is more like that recorded by GHRS, then in our analysis we have overestimated $c_4$.

limitations_admitted.value: The adopted NIR extinction law slope (alpha_NIR = 1.61) is likely imperfect for R136, causing systematic residual patterns in NIR bands and high reduced chi^2 values (dominated by H and K_s bands).

evidence.quote: Upon inspecting the residuals of our fits as a function of $A_V$, we see clear patterns for all NIR bands, indicating that the law is not completely adequate.

evidence.loc: An R_5495-dependent average extinction law for R136
evidence.quote: The $H$ and $K_s$ bands dominate the high $\chi^2$ values: relative to the observational uncertainties the residuals in $H$ and $K_s$ are on average six times larger than in the other bands.

limitations_admitted.value: Lack of observations across the 2175 Å bump prevents fitting the Drude profile parameters directly.

evidence.quote: We do not fit the data of the bump as we lack observations here, and instead adopt the values that (cite: 2003ApJ...594..279G) find for LMC SGS 2

limitations_admitted.value: Inferred initial stellar masses are highly dependent on evolutionary models, chosen observables, and the assumption of single-star evolution rather than stellar mergers.

evidence.quote: We note that initial masses of these stars, both ours and those presented in literature, are highly model dependent (see, e.g. (cite: 2021A&A...647A..13G), (cite: 2022MNRAS.516.4052H), and (cite: 2022arXiv220211080B), their Fig. 17).
Lastly, all these analyses are based on single-star evolution scenarios, but it is important to keep in mind that these very massive stars might be merger products (cite: 2012MNRAS.426.1416B).

referee_caveats_inferred: High reduced chi-squared values (average 18.3, up to 164.3) driven by H and K_s band residuals indicate tension between the VLT/SPHERE NIR photometry or its uncertainties and the adopted Maiz Apellaniz et al. (2014) NIR law.
The 2175 A bump parameters are fixed to values from LMC SGS 2 (Gordon et al. 2003) without local NUV spectroscopy to verify if the bump strength/width varies across R136.
